claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, and 6, run a representation-persistence study on open safety-aligned models with accessible activations, such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Vicuna. Use paired harmful instructions from AdvBench and JailbreakBench in three forms: plain harmful prompt expected to be refused, the same harmful prompt wrapped in successful jailbreak templates or public GCG-style adversarial prompts, and matched benign prompts from Alpaca/XSTest. Decode deterministically and label refusal/compliance with a human-calibrated judge. For each attention head, compare activations and attention outputs across plain-harmful-refused, jailbroken-harmful-complied, and benign conditions; use activation patching/path patching to test whether heads that encode harmfulness in the refused condition still carry similar information in the successful jailbreak condition. Results supporting bypass rather than elimination would show that many harmfulness-sensitive heads remain closer to the plain harmful condition than to benign prompts even when ASR is high, while the downstream refusal behavior changes. Results supporting elimination would show harmfulness-sensitive representations collapsing to benign-like states during successful jailbreaks. If a released activation dataset already demonstrated this persistence across models, attacks, and human-validated success labels, this experiment could be reduced to replication on additional model families.

To address subclaims 4 and 5, identify whether a small subset of attention heads is selectively suppressed by successful jailbreaks and whether suppressing that subset is sufficient to convert refusal into compliance. Starting from the paired runs in Experiment 1, rank heads by jailbreak-induced reduction in output norm, attention contribution, or causal effect on refusal logits using activation patching/ACDC threshold sweeps. Select the smallest high-effect subset and intervene at inference on plain harmful prompts by zeroing or scaling those heads down to their jailbroken activation levels; also perform the inverse intervention by restoring or scaling up those heads during jailbroken prompts. Compare ASR, refusal rate, KL divergence, and harmless-prompt performance against unmodified inference, size-matched random head ablations, and ablations of heads with similar magnitude but low causal score. The claim is supported if targeted suppression alone produces a large refusal-to-compliance shift, random matched ablations do not, restoring the heads reduces jailbreak ASR, and Alpaca/benign performance is not broadly degraded. The claim is weakened if many heads are required, effects match random ablation, or the intervention mainly causes general incoherence. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by stronger prior evidence releasing the exact head set plus dose-response and random-ablation controls across several public benchmarks.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, evaluate whether the persistent internal representations can serve as a no-additional-training harmful-input detector competitive with dedicated safety models. Using only the heads/features identified in Experiments 1 and 2, predefine a direct readout score such as the aggregate activation magnitude or cosine similarity of the persistent harmfulness-representing heads, without fitting a classifier; if a binary threshold is needed, report both threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC and a calibration-only threshold chosen before the held-out test. Evaluate on held-out harmful prompts from AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench, plus benign/ambiguous prompts from Alpaca and XSTest, including both plain and jailbroken variants. Compare against dedicated or commonly used safety systems such as LlamaGuard, WildGuard, OpenAI Moderation where available, and a calibrated GPT-4-class judge, using AUROC, FPR at fixed TPR, precision/recall, and robustness to jailbreak wrappers. The claim is supported if the direct internal readout detects harmful intent in successful jailbreaks with performance close to these safety models and without supervised probe training; it is weakened if performance requires a trained classifier, fails on held-out attacks, or has high benign false positives. This experiment could be made unnecessary if a public benchmark already released the frozen readout rule, held-out prompts, labels, and head activations showing competitive zero-shot detection across models.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct attacked-versus-unattacked comparison of safety-relevant internal signals, across enough of the network to distinguish persistence from global erasure during a verified successful jailbreak.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly compares refused harmful inputs with successful jailbreaks of the same harmful inputs and benign controls, at every attention head, while testing whether the information remains present. Its explicit persistence-versus-collapse outcomes answer the bypass-versus-elimination premise. The omission of an identically named refusal-direction statistic or a particular component decomposition does not prevent the proposed comparison from establishing persistence.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched evaluation corpus containing harmful requests with verified refusal baselines and successful attacked counterparts, so attack effects can be inferred within request pairs rather than from different prompt populations.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 specifies paired harmful instructions in plain and successful-jailbreak forms, with human-calibrated refusal/compliance labels. Proposed experiment 1 starts from those paired runs for causal interventions. The proposed attacks and prompt sources differ from the reference, but the claim requires verified matched successes, not the reference's particular attack mix or sample counts.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level scoring and selection procedure that identifies heads associated with refusal suppression versus persistent harmful-content representation, with sensitivity analysis showing that the selected categories are not artifacts of one arbitrary cutoff.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level causal attribution that separates effects of the original harmful request from effects of the jailbreak wrapper, so head specialization is distinguishable from a generic difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: None of the proposed experiments decomposes head activity by token origin. Proposed 0 compares whole prompts and conditions, while Proposed 1 intervenes on heads and Proposed 2 reads out aggregate features; none can determine whether the contrast is driven specifically by wrapper tokens rather than by different sensitivity to the harmful request.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes attack-template-driven suppression from the rival explanation that the head groups simply have different sensitivity to harmful content.
That distinction requires separating contributions from original harmful-request tokens and jailbreak-template tokens.
The proposed experiments compare complete prompt conditions and head-level interventions, but never perform token-origin attribution.
Therefore their outcomes can show selective head suppression and persistence without resolving what input tokens caused the difference.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn the token-level mechanistic distinction established by reference experiment 5: missing.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would provide strong evidence for persistence in attention-head representations, selective head suppression, causal refusal-to-compliance conversion, and a training-free detector. However, it omits the token-level attribution needed to distinguish the claimed attack-template-specific mechanism from the rival explanation that the head groups merely differ in sensitivity to harmful content. It also leaves the whole-model representation test weaker by omitting MLPs. Consequently, the outcomes would not settle the full mechanistic claim.
missing: Token-level attribution separating original harmful-request tokens from jailbreak-template tokens, with a prespecified comparison between the putative suppressed and persistent head groups.
If the claim is intended as a whole-model statement rather than an attention-head statement, measurements of the safety/refusal signal in MLP components as well as attention heads.
